questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes business ethics?

options.A: The set of laws that a company must obey in the countries in which it trades
options.B: The policies a company adopts to maximise shareholder wealth over the long term
options.C: The application of moral principles and standards of right and wrong to business decisions and behaviour
options.D: The internal rules an organisation sets to make sure staff arrive at work on time

questions.explanation: Business ethics concerns applying moral principles (what is right and wrong) to business conduct. Law sets a minimum standard of behaviour enforced by the state, but ethics often requires more than legal compliance. Wealth maximisation and attendance rules are business objectives or policies, not ethics as such.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: How does ethical behaviour generally relate to legal compliance?

options.A: Anything that is legal is automatically ethical
options.B: Ethics often demands a higher standard than the law, so an action can be legal yet unethical
options.C: Ethics and law cover exactly the same ground in every jurisdiction
options.D: Ethical rules override the law, so an accountant may break the law to act ethically

questions.explanation: The law represents a minimum enforceable standard; ethics goes further and asks what is right. An action can therefore be perfectly lawful but still unethical, for example exploiting a loophole to mislead customers. Ethics does not authorise breaking the law, and law and ethics do not overlap completely.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Why is ethical behaviour particularly important for professional accountants?

options.A: Because ethical accountants are always paid more than other professionals
options.B: Because ethics removes the need for accountants to comply with accounting standards
options.C: Because only accountants are subject to the law of contract
options.D: Because they have a responsibility to act in the public interest, not only to satisfy an individual client or employer

questions.explanation: A distinguishing mark of the accountancy profession is its acceptance of a responsibility to act in the public interest. Users of financial information such as investors, lenders and government rely on accountants' integrity. Ethics supplements technical standards rather than replacing them.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: An accountant believes that following clear, detailed rules is the best way to ensure ethical conduct, because it leaves no room for personal judgement. What is the main weakness of relying only on a rules-based approach to ethics?

options.A: Rules cannot anticipate every situation, so people may comply with the letter of a rule while defeating its purpose
options.B: Rules-based approaches are never enforceable by professional bodies
options.C: Rules-based approaches require too much professional judgement
options.D: Rules cannot be written down and so cannot be communicated to members

questions.explanation: A rules-based system cannot foresee every circumstance and encourages a 'tick-box' mentality in which people look for loopholes. A principles-based approach, such as the conceptual framework in the CIMA Code of Ethics, requires members to apply fundamental principles to any situation. Rules are enforceable and easy to communicate, and it is principles, not rules, that require more judgement.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of a principles-based approach to professional ethics?

options.A: Members are given an exhaustive list of prohibited actions and anything not listed is permitted
options.B: Members follow fixed procedures and do not need to exercise judgement
options.C: Members are only bound by ethical requirements that are also criminal offences
options.D: Members must identify, evaluate and address threats to the fundamental principles in each situation they face

questions.explanation: Under a principles-based (conceptual framework) approach, members apply the fundamental principles to their own circumstances by identifying threats, evaluating them and addressing them with safeguards. An exhaustive list of prohibited actions and fixed procedures describe a rules-based approach. Ethical requirements go beyond the criminal law.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Which of the following personal qualities is most closely associated with 'professional scepticism'?

options.A: Distrusting every client and assuming that all management representations are false
options.B: Refusing to rely on the work of any other professional
options.C: Having a questioning mind and critically assessing evidence rather than accepting it at face value
options.D: Following management's instructions without question to save time

questions.explanation: Professional scepticism means maintaining a questioning mind and critically assessing the evidence obtained, being alert to conditions that may indicate misstatement. It does not mean assuming dishonesty in everyone. Blindly following instructions is the opposite of scepticism.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: An accountant is described as having 'independence in appearance'. What does this mean?

options.A: Avoiding facts and circumstances so significant that a reasonable and informed third party would conclude that objectivity had been compromised
options.B: Having a state of mind that permits an opinion to be expressed without being affected by influences that compromise judgement
options.C: Being employed by a different organisation from the one being reported on
options.D: Holding no shares in any listed company

questions.explanation: Independence in appearance concerns how a situation looks to a reasonable and informed third party: circumstances that would lead such a person to doubt the accountant's objectivity must be avoided. The state of mind description is independence of mind. Being employed elsewhere or holding no shares are not the definition, although they may help.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best example of an organisation acting with social responsibility rather than merely complying with the law?

options.A: Paying employees the legal minimum wage
options.B: Voluntarily reducing waste and emissions below the levels permitted by regulation
options.C: Filing annual accounts by the statutory deadline
options.D: Deducting income tax from employees' pay as required by law

questions.explanation: Social responsibility involves going beyond legal obligations to act in the interests of society and the environment. Cutting emissions below legal limits is voluntary. Paying the minimum wage, filing accounts on time and deducting tax are legal requirements, so they show compliance rather than social responsibility.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: A finance manager discovers that a new cost-cutting plan is fully legal but will mislead customers about the durability of a product. The managing director says: 'If it is legal, it is not our problem.' Which statement best evaluates the managing director's view?

options.A: It is correct because a professional accountant's only duty is to ensure that the law is obeyed
options.B: It is flawed because legality is a minimum standard and the plan conflicts with the principle of integrity, which requires being straightforward and honest
options.C: It is correct because ethical principles only apply to the preparation of financial statements
options.D: It is flawed because any misleading statement is automatically a criminal offence

questions.explanation: Legal compliance does not make conduct ethical; the law is only a minimum standard. Knowingly being associated with misleading information breaches the principle of integrity, and accountants' ethical duties apply to all their professional activities, not just financial statements. Not every misleading statement is a crime, so the claim that it is automatically an offence overstates the position.

questions.topic: Business ethics and the role of the professional accountant
questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains why professional bodies such as CIMA require members to undertake continuing professional development (CPD)?

options.A: To ensure that members earn enough income to remain independent of clients
options.B: To replace the need for members to comply with the fundamental principles
options.C: To demonstrate integrity by recording the number of hours spent in training
options.D: To maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level required to provide competent professional services, supporting the principle of professional competence and due care

questions.explanation: The principle of professional competence and due care requires members to attain and maintain professional knowledge and skill so that clients and employers receive competent service. CPD is the mechanism for keeping that knowledge up to date as standards, law and technology change. It supports, rather than replaces, the other principles and is not mainly about income or hours recorded.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the five fundamental principles in the CIMA Code of Ethics?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Independence
options.D: Confidentiality

questions.explanation: The five fundamental principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour. Independence is an important related concept, especially for those providing assurance services, but it is not itself listed as one of the five fundamental principles.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: Which fundamental principle requires a member to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional behaviour
options.D: Professional competence and due care

questions.explanation: Integrity means being straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships, and implies fair dealing and truthfulness. Objectivity concerns avoiding bias, conflicts of interest and undue influence. Professional behaviour concerns complying with laws and avoiding discredit to the profession.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: Which fundamental principle is breached when a management accountant allows a close friendship with a supplier to bias her recommendation on which supplier to use?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional competence and due care
options.D: Professional behaviour

questions.explanation: Objectivity requires that a member does not allow bias, conflict of interest or the undue influence of others to override professional judgement. Allowing a friendship to bias a recommendation is a clear failure of objectivity. The other principles concern secrecy of information, competence and reputation of the profession.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: A management accountant is asked to prepare a complex tax computation for her employer even though she has no tax training and there is no time to obtain help. Which fundamental principle is most threatened?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Confidentiality
options.C: Professional competence and due care
options.D: Objectivity

questions.explanation: Professional competence and due care requires members to act diligently and to undertake only work they have the knowledge and skill to perform, or to obtain appropriate help. Taking on a task outside her expertise without support threatens this principle. There is no suggestion of dishonesty, disclosure of information or bias.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: In which of the following situations may a member disclose confidential information without breaching the principle of confidentiality?

options.A: When disclosure is required by law, for example in response to a court order
options.B: When a former employer's information would help the member in a new job
options.C: When a friend asks for the information for personal investment purposes
options.D: When the member believes that the information is already rumoured in the market

questions.explanation: The Code permits disclosure where it is required by law (such as a court order or anti-money-laundering reporting), permitted by law and authorised by the client or employer, or where there is a professional duty or right to disclose. Using information for personal advantage or that of third parties is prohibited, and a rumour does not make information public.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: A member who moves to a new employer uses detailed pricing information from his previous employer to help his new employer undercut it. Which statement is correct?

options.A: He does not breach confidentiality, because the duty ends when employment ends
options.B: He breaches objectivity, but not confidentiality
options.C: He does not breach any principle, because he is acting in his new employer's interests
options.D: He breaches confidentiality, because the duty continues after the employment relationship has ended

questions.explanation: The duty of confidentiality continues even after the end of a relationship between a member and a client or employer. A member may use general experience and expertise gained, but must not use or disclose confidential information acquired from a previous employer. Acting in the new employer's interest does not justify the breach.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: A member posts on social media that a rival accounting firm's staff are 'incompetent crooks', without any evidence. Which fundamental principle is most directly breached?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Professional behaviour
options.C: Objectivity
options.D: Professional competence and due care

questions.explanation: Professional behaviour requires compliance with relevant laws and regulations and avoidance of any action that discredits the profession. Making disparaging, unsupported claims about others' work is specifically inconsistent with this principle. No confidential information, bias in judgement or technical competence is involved.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: Which of the following is included in the principle of professional competence and due care?

options.A: Never accepting gifts or hospitality from clients
options.B: Keeping all business information secret in every circumstance
options.C: Acting diligently in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards
options.D: Ensuring that the employer achieves its profit targets

questions.explanation: Professional competence and due care has two elements: attaining and maintaining professional knowledge and skill, and acting diligently in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards. Gifts relate to objectivity threats, confidentiality is a separate principle with exceptions, and profit targets are not an ethical principle.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: A member knowingly signs off a management report that omits a material loss, although every figure that IS in the report is accurate. Which statement is correct?

options.A: No principle is breached, because all the figures included are accurate
options.B: Only confidentiality is breached, because the loss was kept secret
options.C: Only professional competence is breached, because the report is incomplete by mistake
options.D: Integrity is breached, because a member must not be associated with information that omits or obscures information where the omission would be misleading

questions.explanation: Integrity requires that a member is not knowingly associated with reports or information that contain materially false or misleading statements, statements furnished recklessly, or that omit or obscure required information where this would be misleading. Accurate figures do not cure a misleading omission. The omission was knowing, so it is not merely a competence error.

questions.topic: The CIMA Code of Ethics: fundamental principles
questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the 'reasonable and informed third party' test used in the CIMA Code of Ethics?

options.A: It asks whether a hypothetical person with relevant knowledge, weighing all the specific facts known to the member, would be likely to reach the same conclusions
options.B: It asks whether the member's line manager agrees with the member's decision
options.C: It asks whether a court would find the member liable in negligence
options.D: It asks whether a majority of the public, without any specialist knowledge, would approve of the decision

questions.explanation: The test considers whether the same conclusions would probably be reached by another party who has the relevant knowledge and experience to understand and evaluate the appropriateness of the member's conclusions, weighing all the relevant facts. It is an objective benchmark, not the view of a manager, a court or an uninformed public.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the categories of threat to compliance with the fundamental principles identified in the CIMA Code of Ethics?

options.A: Self-interest threat
options.B: Self-confidence threat
options.C: Advocacy threat
options.D: Familiarity threat

questions.explanation: The categories of threat are self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation. 'Self-confidence' is not a recognised category. Questions often use plausible-sounding but invented threat names as distractors.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: A management accountant's annual bonus depends on the profit figure that she herself calculates. Which type of threat does this create?

options.A: Self-review threat
options.B: Advocacy threat
options.C: Intimidation threat
options.D: Self-interest threat

questions.explanation: A self-interest threat arises where a financial or other interest will inappropriately influence the member's judgement or behaviour. A bonus linked to a figure the member prepares gives her a financial interest in that figure. There is no review of her own earlier work, promotion of a position or pressure from others.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: A finance director tells a junior accountant that he will be dismissed unless he agrees to a particular accounting treatment. Which threat is present?

options.A: Familiarity threat
options.B: Self-review threat
options.C: Intimidation threat
options.D: Advocacy threat

questions.explanation: An intimidation threat arises where a member is deterred from acting objectively by actual or perceived pressures, including threats of dismissal. The junior accountant is being pressured to give in. Familiarity involves sympathy arising from a long or close relationship, which is not described.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: An accountant is asked to evaluate the effectiveness of a costing system that she designed and implemented last year. Which threat arises?

options.A: Self-review threat
options.B: Self-interest threat
options.C: Familiarity threat
options.D: Intimidation threat

questions.explanation: A self-review threat arises when a member must re-evaluate a previous judgement or work they performed, because they are unlikely to identify their own errors objectively. Here she is reviewing her own system design. Other threats may also be present, but self-review is the most direct.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: A management accountant is asked to speak publicly in support of her employer's position in a dispute with a regulator. Which threat is most likely to arise?

options.A: Self-review threat
options.B: Intimidation threat
options.C: Advocacy threat
options.D: Familiarity threat

questions.explanation: An advocacy threat arises when a member promotes a client's or employer's position to the point that objectivity is compromised. Publicly championing the employer's case in a dispute is advocacy. The member is not reviewing her own work or being directly pressured.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: A purchasing accountant has dealt with the same supplier's sales director for twelve years and they now holiday together. Which threat is created?

options.A: Advocacy threat
options.B: Familiarity threat
options.C: Self-review threat
options.D: Self-interest threat

questions.explanation: A familiarity threat arises when, because of a long or close relationship, a member becomes too sympathetic to another's interests or too accepting of their work. A long-standing personal friendship with a supplier is a classic example. Safeguards could include rotating responsibility for that supplier.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: Under the conceptual framework in the CIMA Code of Ethics, what should a member do first when facing a situation that might compromise a fundamental principle?

options.A: Identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles
options.B: Resign immediately from the engagement or employment
options.C: Report the matter to the police
options.D: Apply a safeguard before considering whether a threat exists

questions.explanation: The conceptual framework requires the member to identify threats, evaluate whether they are at an acceptable level, and address them by eliminating them or reducing them to an acceptable level with safeguards. Resignation is a last resort, and safeguards can only be chosen once the threat is identified and evaluated.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: The CIMA Code of Ethics recognises that conditions, policies and procedures that help a member comply with the fundamental principles may be established either by the profession, legislation or regulation, or by the member's employing organisation. Which of the following is established by the profession, legislation or regulation rather than by the employing organisation?

options.A: The employer's own whistleblowing hotline
options.B: A company's internal policy on accepting gifts
options.C: An employer's internal review of work by a second accountant
options.D: Mandatory continuing professional development requirements

questions.explanation: Conditions, policies and procedures established by the profession, legislation or regulation include educational, training and experience requirements, continuing professional development (CPD) requirements, professional standards, professional or regulatory monitoring and disciplinary procedures, and corporate governance regulation. A whistleblowing hotline, a gifts policy and an internal second review are set up by the employer itself. Older editions of the Code grouped these as 'safeguards created by the profession, legislation or regulation' and 'safeguards in the work environment'; the current Code no longer uses those headings, but the distinction between the source of each measure still holds.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: A member's employer offers him a luxury holiday 'as thanks' just before he finalises a valuation that will determine the employer's loan covenant compliance. After evaluating the threat as significant, which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Accept the holiday but disclose it in a note to the valuation
options.B: Decline the offer, because the threat to objectivity cannot be reduced to an acceptable level while it is accepted
options.C: Accept the holiday, because gifts from an employer cannot create threats
options.D: Accept the holiday and ask a colleague to sign the valuation instead, without telling anyone why

questions.explanation: A valuable gift timed to coincide with a key judgement creates a self-interest threat to objectivity, and the Code's guidance on inducements says that an offer made with the intent of improperly influencing behaviour should be declined. Where the threat cannot be eliminated or reduced to an acceptable level, the member should not accept. Disclosure alone does not remove the influence, gifts from an employer can create threats just like gifts from anyone else, and quietly passing the work to a colleague without explanation is not a transparent safeguard.

questions.topic: Threats to the fundamental principles and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which statement about safeguards is correct?

options.A: Every threat can always be eliminated by an appropriate safeguard
options.B: Safeguards are only required for members in public practice, not members in business
options.C: Once a safeguard is applied, the member need not reconsider the threat even if circumstances change
options.D: Where no safeguard can reduce a threat to an acceptable level, the member should decline or end the specific activity, or in extreme cases resign

questions.explanation: The Code recognises that some threats are so significant that no safeguard is adequate; the member must then decline or discontinue the activity, or resign. The conceptual framework applies to both members in practice and members in business. Threats must be re-evaluated if new information or changed circumstances arise.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: What is the first step a member should normally take when trying to resolve an ethical conflict?

options.A: Gather the relevant facts and identify the ethical issues and fundamental principles involved
options.B: Resign from the organisation
options.C: Inform a journalist so that the issue becomes public
options.D: Ignore the issue unless it involves a criminal offence

questions.explanation: The Code's resolution process begins with establishing the relevant facts, the ethical issues and the fundamental principles involved, followed by considering internal procedures and alternative courses of action. Resignation is a last resort. Going to the media is not an appropriate first step and may itself breach confidentiality.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best description of 'whistleblowing'?

options.A: Leaking a company's confidential plans to a competitor for payment
options.B: Refusing to work overtime without extra pay
options.C: Disclosing information about wrongdoing within an organisation to someone who can take action, internally or externally
options.D: Publishing an organisation's annual report

questions.explanation: Whistleblowing is reporting suspected wrongdoing, such as fraud, danger or illegal conduct, to people able to address it, whether internal (such as an audit committee) or external (such as a regulator). Selling secrets to a competitor is a breach of confidentiality, not whistleblowing.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: Which is the correct order of the three stages of money laundering?

options.A: Placement, layering, integration
options.B: Layering, placement, integration
options.C: Integration, layering, placement
options.D: Placement, integration, layering

questions.explanation: Placement introduces criminal cash into the financial system, layering disguises its origin through complex transactions, and integration returns the funds to the economy as apparently legitimate wealth. The order matters: funds must be placed before they can be layered and finally integrated.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: A criminal pays cash from drug sales into many small bank deposits below reporting thresholds. Which stage of money laundering does this represent?

options.A: Layering
options.B: Integration
options.C: Placement
options.D: Tipping off

questions.explanation: Placement is the initial stage in which illicit cash is introduced into the financial system, often by splitting it into small deposits ('smurfing'). Layering would involve moving the money through complex transactions, and integration would return it as apparently clean funds. Tipping off is a separate offence, not a stage.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: Under UK anti-money-laundering law, an accountant who suspects money laundering tells the client that a report has been made to the authorities. Which offence may the accountant have committed?

options.A: Placement
options.B: Tipping off
options.C: Insider dealing
options.D: Fraudulent trading

questions.explanation: Tipping off is the offence of disclosing that a suspicious activity report has been made, or that an investigation is under way or contemplated, where the disclosure is likely to prejudice an investigation (Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, s333A, which applies to the UK regulated sector, including accountants). Placement is a stage of laundering, and insider dealing and fraudulent trading are unrelated offences.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: An accountant in business suspects that a colleague is laundering money through the company's accounts. To whom should she normally report her suspicion first?

options.A: The colleague suspected of laundering
options.B: The company's external customers
options.C: A national newspaper
options.D: The organisation's money laundering reporting officer (MLRO) or nominated officer

questions.explanation: Organisations within the regulated sector appoint an MLRO (nominated officer) to receive internal reports and decide whether to report externally to the relevant authority. Reporting to the suspect would risk tipping off, and disclosure to customers or the press would breach confidentiality and could prejudice an investigation.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: A member has exhausted internal procedures and the ethical conflict remains unresolved. Which of the following would be an appropriate next step under the CIMA Code?

options.A: Continue with the unethical action because the internal procedures have been completed
options.B: Disclose the matter to friends and family to obtain their opinion
options.C: Seek advice from CIMA's ethics helpline or obtain legal advice before deciding whether to disassociate from the matter
options.D: Destroy any documents relating to the matter

questions.explanation: If a conflict cannot be resolved internally, the member may seek professional advice from CIMA or legal advice, and if still unresolved should refuse to remain associated with the matter, which could ultimately mean resignation. Proceeding with the unethical action, discussing confidential matters socially or destroying evidence would all be inappropriate.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: In the UK, which of the following statements about legal protection for whistleblowers is correct?

options.A: Only employees with at least ten years' service are protected
options.B: Protection applies only when the disclosure is made to a newspaper
options.C: A whistleblower must prove that the wrongdoing actually occurred to be protected
options.D: Workers who make a protected disclosure about specified wrongdoing are protected from dismissal and detriment for making it

questions.explanation: Under UK law (the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, which inserted Part IVA and related provisions into the Employment Rights Act 1996), workers who make a qualifying disclosure in the public interest, for example about crimes, breaches of legal obligations or danger to health and safety, are protected from detriment, and dismissal for making a protected disclosure is automatically unfair (ERA 1996, s103A) with no minimum service requirement. A reasonable belief is required, not proof, and disclosures to the employer or a prescribed regulator are protected more readily than disclosures to the media.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: A management accountant's manager instructs her to reclassify revenue expenditure as capital expenditure so that a profit target is met. She raises it with the manager, who refuses to change his mind. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Escalate the matter to a higher level of management or the audit committee, in line with the organisation's procedures
options.B: Make the adjustment, because she has already raised her concern
options.C: Report the matter immediately to the press
options.D: Resign immediately without raising the matter with anyone else

questions.explanation: Where a matter cannot be resolved with the immediate superior, the member should escalate it through the organisation's procedures, for example to the next level of management, internal audit or the audit committee. Complying would breach integrity. Going to the press is premature and resignation is a last resort after internal routes and advice have been exhausted.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict, whistleblowing and money laundering
questions.question_text: Which of the following situations is most likely to involve the 'layering' stage of money laundering?

options.A: Depositing banknotes from criminal activity into a bank account
options.B: Repeatedly transferring funds between shell companies in several countries to obscure the audit trail
options.C: Buying a property using funds that now appear to be legitimate business profits
options.D: Reporting a suspicious transaction to the authorities

questions.explanation: Layering involves complex series of transactions, often across borders and through shell companies, designed to distance the funds from their criminal source. Depositing cash is placement, and buying assets with apparently clean funds is integration. Reporting is a compliance action, not laundering.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines corporate governance?

options.A: The process of preparing a company's financial statements
options.B: The government's regulation of competition between companies
options.C: The system by which companies are directed and controlled
options.D: The day-to-day management of a company's production function

questions.explanation: Corporate governance is widely defined as the system by which companies are directed and controlled. Boards of directors are responsible for governance, and shareholders appoint the directors and auditors to satisfy themselves that an appropriate structure is in place. Financial reporting and operations are parts of what is governed, not the definition.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: In agency theory as applied to a listed company, who are the principals and who are the agents?

options.A: Directors are principals and shareholders are agents
options.B: Shareholders are principals and directors are agents
options.C: Employees are principals and customers are agents
options.D: Auditors are principals and directors are agents

questions.explanation: Agency theory views shareholders (owners) as principals who delegate the running of the company to directors (agents). Because of the separation of ownership and control, the agents may pursue their own interests, and governance mechanisms aim to align the two.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: What does 'comply or explain' mean in the context of a principles-based governance code?

options.A: Companies must comply with every provision or face criminal penalties
options.B: Directors must explain every decision to shareholders before taking it
options.C: Companies may ignore the code if they explain this verbally to the regulator
options.D: Companies either follow the code's provisions or explain in their annual report why they have not done so

questions.explanation: Under a comply-or-explain approach, such as the UK Corporate Governance Code for listed companies, companies disclose whether they have complied with the code and give reasons for any departure. Shareholders then judge whether the explanation is acceptable. It is not a criminal regime like a rules-based statute.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of an agency cost?

options.A: The cost of an external audit commissioned to monitor the directors' stewardship
options.B: The cost of raw materials used in production
options.C: The interest paid on a bank loan
options.D: The cost of advertising a new product

questions.explanation: Agency costs are costs incurred by principals to monitor and control agents, plus any loss from agents acting in their own interests. Audit fees, governance structures and incentive schemes are typical examples. Raw materials, interest and advertising are normal business costs not caused by the agency relationship.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic of a rules-based approach to corporate governance, as exemplified by the US Sarbanes-Oxley Act?

options.A: Companies are free to depart from requirements if they explain why
options.B: Governance principles are voluntary guidance with no enforcement
options.C: It relies mainly on shareholders deciding whether explanations are adequate
options.D: Governance requirements are set in law and non-compliance can attract legal penalties

questions.explanation: A rules-based approach makes governance requirements legally binding, so failure to comply can lead to penalties. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act in the US is the usual example. The other options describe a principles-based, comply-or-explain approach.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an advantage of a principles-based approach to corporate governance compared with a rules-based approach?

options.A: It gives investors certainty that every company follows identical practices
options.B: It removes the need for any disclosure in the annual report
options.C: It is flexible, allowing companies to adapt practices to their own circumstances
options.D: It eliminates the risk that companies will give poor explanations for non-compliance

questions.explanation: Principles-based codes are flexible and can be applied sensibly to companies of different sizes and circumstances. The drawback is less certainty and the risk of boilerplate or weak explanations. Disclosure is central to comply-or-explain, so it is not removed.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: An 'insider' system of corporate ownership, common in parts of continental Europe and Asia, is characterised by which of the following?

options.A: Widely dispersed ownership by many small investors trading on a stock market
options.B: Ownership concentrated in families, banks or other companies with close links to management
options.C: Companies owned exclusively by their employees
options.D: Companies owned and run by the state

questions.explanation: Insider systems feature concentrated ownership by families, banks, other companies or founders who are close to management, which reduces some agency problems but can disadvantage minority shareholders. Outsider systems, typical of the UK and US, have widely dispersed shareholdings.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as a stakeholder of a company?

options.A: The shareholders of an unrelated company in a different industry, which has no dealings with the company
options.B: Employees
options.C: Suppliers
options.D: The local community

questions.explanation: Stakeholders are groups or individuals who affect, or are affected by, the organisation's activities, such as employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, government and local communities. Shareholders of a company in an unrelated industry have no meaningful interest in or influence over the company.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: The OECD Principles of Corporate Governance include the equitable treatment of shareholders. Which practice would most clearly breach this principle?

options.A: Issuing shares with different rights where the rights are disclosed to investors
options.B: Holding a general meeting at which all shareholders may vote
options.C: Publishing price-sensitive information to all shareholders at the same time
options.D: Allowing directors to trade in the company's shares using undisclosed price-sensitive information

questions.explanation: Equitable treatment requires that all shareholders, including minority and foreign shareholders, are treated fairly and that insider trading and abusive self-dealing are prohibited. Directors trading on undisclosed information benefit at other shareholders' expense. Disclosed differences in class rights, open meetings and simultaneous disclosure are consistent with the principle.

questions.topic: Corporate governance: principles and approaches
questions.question_text: A company has a two-tier board structure. Which statement correctly describes it?

options.A: Executive and non-executive directors sit together on a single board with collective responsibility
options.B: A supervisory board, which may include employee representatives, oversees a separate management board that runs the business
options.C: The chair and chief executive are always the same person
options.D: There are two boards with identical membership that meet on alternate months

questions.explanation: In a two-tier structure, common in Germany, a supervisory board (often including employee representatives) appoints and monitors a separate management board of executives. A single board of executive and non-executive directors is a unitary board, as used in the UK. The roles of the two tiers are distinct, so membership is not identical.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Why do corporate governance codes recommend that the roles of chair and chief executive should not be held by the same individual?

options.A: To avoid unfettered powers of decision being concentrated in one person
options.B: To reduce the total salary cost of the board
options.C: Because the law prohibits a single person from holding two offices
options.D: Because the chief executive must always be a non-executive director

questions.explanation: Splitting the roles ensures a clear division of responsibility between running the board (chair) and running the business (chief executive), so no one individual has unchecked power. It is a governance recommendation rather than a general legal prohibition, and the chief executive is an executive director.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key role of non-executive directors?

options.A: To run the day-to-day operations of the company
options.B: To prepare the company's monthly management accounts
options.C: To scrutinise and constructively challenge the performance of management
options.D: To act as the company's external auditor

questions.explanation: Non-executive directors contribute an independent view, constructively challenge strategy and scrutinise management performance, as well as overseeing risk, remuneration and appointments. Day-to-day operations and management accounts are executive responsibilities, and external audit must be independent of the board.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Which board committee normally takes the lead in reviewing the integrity of the financial statements and the relationship with the external auditor?

options.A: Remuneration committee
options.B: Nomination committee
options.C: Audit committee
options.D: Executive committee

questions.explanation: The audit committee monitors the integrity of financial statements, reviews internal controls and the internal audit function, and oversees the appointment, independence and effectiveness of the external auditor. Remuneration and nomination committees deal with pay and board appointments respectively.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Which of the following would most likely cause a non-executive director to be regarded as NOT independent?

options.A: He holds a non-executive role in an unrelated company
options.B: He receives a fixed fee for his services as a non-executive director
options.C: He has extensive experience in the company's industry
options.D: He was an executive employee of the company until two years ago

questions.explanation: Governance codes treat recent employment by the company as a circumstance likely to impair independence, because the director may be too close to current management; the UK Corporate Governance Code, for example, refers to having been an employee of the company within the last five years. Holding other unrelated roles, receiving a fixed fee and having industry experience do not of themselves impair independence.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of a remuneration committee composed of independent non-executive directors?

options.A: To set the pay of all employees in the company
options.B: To ensure that no director is involved in deciding his or her own remuneration
options.C: To approve the company's annual budget
options.D: To appoint the external auditor

questions.explanation: A key governance principle is that no director should decide their own pay. The remuneration committee of independent non-executives sets executive director remuneration policy, aiming to link it to long-term performance. Employee pay generally, budgets and auditor appointment are outside its core role.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a primary responsibility of the nomination committee?

options.A: Leading the process for board appointments and planning succession
options.B: Monitoring the effectiveness of the internal audit function
options.C: Determining the dividend to be paid to shareholders
options.D: Approving the external auditor's fee

questions.explanation: The nomination committee leads the process for appointments to the board, considers the balance of skills, experience and diversity, and plans orderly succession. Internal audit oversight and auditor fees belong to the audit committee, and dividends are a board decision.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Which of the following is generally regarded as good practice for the remuneration of non-executive directors?

options.A: Fees reflecting time commitment and responsibilities, without performance-related elements such as share options
options.B: Large bonuses linked to annual profit targets
options.C: Share options that vest when the share price rises
options.D: No payment at all, so that they remain fully independent

questions.explanation: Governance codes recommend that non-executive remuneration reflects time commitment and responsibilities and should not include share options or other performance-related elements, as these could compromise independence. Paying nothing would make it hard to attract capable people and is not required.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: Why are board evaluations recommended by corporate governance codes?

options.A: To determine the market value of the company's shares
options.B: To review the performance of the board, its committees and individual directors and identify improvements
options.C: To decide which shareholders may vote at the annual general meeting
options.D: To replace the need for external audit

questions.explanation: Formal and rigorous evaluation of the board, its committees, the chair and individual directors helps identify weaknesses in composition, skills or processes and supports re-election decisions. It has nothing to do with share valuation, voting rights or external audit.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: A listed company's audit committee consists of the finance director, the chief executive and one independent non-executive director. Which criticism is most valid?

options.A: The committee is too independent, because it should be chaired by the finance director
options.B: There is no problem, because the finance director has the most relevant financial expertise
options.C: The committee should include the external audit partner as a voting member
options.D: The committee lacks independence, because it should be made up of independent non-executive directors

questions.explanation: Governance codes expect the audit committee of a listed company to comprise independent non-executive directors, at least one with recent and relevant financial experience. Executives on the committee would be overseeing their own work, a self-review problem. The external auditor attends to report but must not be a member, to preserve independence.

questions.topic: The board of directors and board committees
questions.question_text: The senior independent director (SID) of a listed company is most likely to be expected to do which of the following?

options.A: Run the company's operations when the chief executive is absent
options.B: Chair the audit committee and sign the audit report
options.C: Act as a sounding board for the chair and an intermediary for other directors and shareholders when normal channels have failed
options.D: Approve all related-party transactions without board involvement

questions.explanation: The SID provides a sounding board for the chair, serves as an intermediary for the other directors and is available to shareholders when contact through the chair or executives has failed or is inappropriate. The SID also typically leads the evaluation of the chair. Running operations, signing audit reports and bypassing the board are not SID functions.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the five components of internal control in the COSO framework?

options.A: Control environment
options.B: Risk assessment
options.C: Monitoring activities
options.D: Strategic planning

questions.explanation: The COSO components are control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities. Strategic planning is a management process but is not one of the five internal control components.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Who is ultimately responsible for a company's system of internal control?

options.A: The board of directors
options.B: The external auditor
options.C: The internal auditor
options.D: The shareholders

questions.explanation: The board is responsible for the company's risk management and internal control systems and for reviewing their effectiveness. Internal audit evaluates controls and reports to the board or audit committee, and the external auditor considers controls for the audit, but neither is responsible for them.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Requiring two separate people to authorise and record a payment is an example of which type of control?

options.A: Physical control
options.B: Arithmetic control
options.C: Segregation of duties
options.D: Supervision control

questions.explanation: Segregation of duties splits authorising, recording and custody between different people, so that one person cannot both commit and conceal an error or fraud. Physical controls protect assets, arithmetic controls check calculations, and supervision is oversight by a manager.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the 'control environment'?

options.A: The specific procedures such as reconciliations and authorisations
options.B: The overall attitude, awareness and actions of directors and management regarding internal control, including 'tone at the top'
options.C: The computer systems used to record transactions
options.D: The external auditor's assessment of risk

questions.explanation: The control environment is the foundation of internal control, covering management's philosophy and operating style, integrity and ethical values, organisational structure and commitment to competence. Reconciliations and authorisations are control activities. IT systems and auditor assessments are not the control environment itself.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key difference between internal audit and external audit?

options.A: Internal audit is required by law for all companies, but external audit is optional
options.B: External audit gives an opinion on the financial statements to shareholders, whereas internal audit is an appraisal function serving management and the board
options.C: External auditors are employees of the company, whereas internal auditors are always external firms
options.D: Internal audit gives an opinion on the truth and fairness of the financial statements

questions.explanation: External auditors report to shareholders on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. Internal audit is an independent appraisal function established by the organisation to review risk management, controls and operations for management and the audit committee. Internal audit is not universally required by law, and external auditors must be independent of the company.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: To whom should the head of internal audit ideally have direct access in order to protect independence?

options.A: The finance director only
options.B: The sales director
options.C: The company's bank
options.D: The audit committee

questions.explanation: Internal audit independence is supported by a direct reporting line to the audit committee, so that findings about the finance function or senior executives cannot be suppressed. Reporting only to the finance director would create a conflict where internal audit reviews finance department controls.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a limitation of any system of internal control?

options.A: Controls eliminate all risk of error once in place
options.B: Controls make the external audit unnecessary
options.C: Controls can be overridden by management or circumvented by collusion
options.D: Controls cannot be documented

questions.explanation: Internal control provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance. Limitations include human error, collusion between staff, management override and the cost of controls exceeding benefits. Controls do not remove all risk or replace external audit, and they can be documented.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which of the following describes a 'detective' control?

options.A: A monthly bank reconciliation that identifies unrecorded or incorrect transactions
options.B: Requiring passwords before staff can access the payroll system
options.C: Training staff before they process invoices
options.D: Locking inventory in a secure warehouse

questions.explanation: Detective controls identify errors or irregularities after they have occurred, such as reconciliations and exception reports. Passwords, training and physical locks are preventive controls designed to stop problems happening in the first place.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: A company's purchase ledger clerk can set up new suppliers, approve invoices and make payments. Which risk is greatest and which control would best address it?

options.A: Overstated sales; introduce sequentially numbered sales invoices
options.B: Payments to fictitious suppliers; segregate supplier set-up, approval and payment between different staff
options.C: Theft of inventory; install CCTV in the warehouse
options.D: Errors in depreciation; require an annual impairment review

questions.explanation: When one person controls the whole purchasing and payment cycle, they could create a fictitious supplier and pay it without detection. Segregating supplier set-up, authorisation and payment is the key control. The other options address unrelated risks in the sales, inventory and non-current asset cycles.

questions.topic: Internal control, risk and audit
questions.question_text: Which statement about the board's responsibility for risk management in a listed company is most consistent with good governance practice?

options.A: The board should delegate all responsibility for risk to the external auditor
options.B: The board need only consider risk when the company makes a loss
options.C: The board should aim to eliminate all business risk
options.D: The board should determine the nature and extent of the principal risks it is willing to take and review the effectiveness of risk management and internal control at least annually

questions.explanation: Governance codes require the board to determine the principal risks it is willing to take in pursuing objectives (its risk appetite), maintain sound risk management and internal control systems and review their effectiveness at least annually. Responsibility cannot be delegated to the auditor, and risk cannot and should not be eliminated, since taking risk is needed to earn returns.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes corporate social responsibility (CSR)?

options.A: The voluntary commitment of a business to act ethically and contribute to economic development while improving the quality of life of employees, communities and society
options.B: A legal duty to maximise profits for shareholders
options.C: A tax charged on large companies by government
options.D: The obligation to publish audited financial statements

questions.explanation: CSR refers to an organisation taking responsibility for the impact of its activities on stakeholders and society beyond legal minimums. It is largely voluntary. Profit maximisation, taxes and audited accounts are legal or economic obligations, not CSR.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: The 'triple bottom line' requires organisations to report on which three dimensions of performance?

options.A: Revenue, costs and profit
options.B: Assets, liabilities and equity
options.C: Economic, social and environmental
options.D: Shareholders, directors and auditors

questions.explanation: The triple bottom line, associated with John Elkington, broadens reporting from purely financial results to economic (profit), social (people) and environmental (planet) performance. The other options are financial statement elements or governance parties.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: In Carroll's pyramid of corporate social responsibility, which responsibility forms the base of the pyramid?

options.A: Philanthropic responsibility
options.B: Ethical responsibility
options.C: Legal responsibility
options.D: Economic responsibility

questions.explanation: Carroll's pyramid has four levels: economic (be profitable) at the base, then legal (obey the law), ethical (do what is right and fair) and philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen) at the top. A business must be economically viable to fulfil the higher responsibilities.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Which view of CSR is most closely associated with the economist Milton Friedman?

options.A: Businesses should give a fixed percentage of profit to charity
options.B: Managers must balance the interests of all stakeholders equally
options.C: The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits, within the rules of the game
options.D: Businesses have no obligation even to obey the law

questions.explanation: Friedman argued that the main social responsibility of business is to use its resources to increase profits, provided it stays within the rules of the game, meaning open and free competition without deception or fraud. He did not argue that businesses can ignore the law, and the balancing of stakeholder interests reflects stakeholder theory.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: A manufacturer pays suppliers in developing countries a fair price, monitors their labour conditions and refuses to use child labour. Which area of CSR does this primarily address?

options.A: Shareholder dividend policy
options.B: Responsible supply chain management and human rights
options.C: Capital structure
options.D: Tax planning

questions.explanation: Ensuring fair dealing with suppliers and acceptable labour conditions throughout the supply chain is a central part of CSR concerning human rights and ethical sourcing. Dividends, capital structure and tax planning are financial decisions with little direct link to these issues.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best example of sustainable business practice?

options.A: Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
options.B: Maximising short-term output regardless of resource depletion
options.C: Expanding into as many markets as possible each year
options.D: Keeping prices constant for as long as possible

questions.explanation: Sustainability, as defined by the Brundtland Report, means development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Practices that deplete resources for short-term output are unsustainable, and market expansion and price stability are unrelated concepts.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a likely business benefit of a strong CSR policy?

options.A: Improved reputation, helping to attract customers, employees and investors
options.B: Guaranteed exemption from environmental legislation
options.C: Elimination of all competition in the market
options.D: Removal of the need for corporate governance

questions.explanation: Effective CSR can strengthen brand reputation, customer loyalty, staff recruitment and retention, and access to capital from responsible investors. It does not exempt a company from law, eliminate competitors or replace governance requirements.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Which stakeholder theory approach holds that managers should consider stakeholder interests because doing so will ultimately improve long-term financial performance?

options.A: The normative view
options.B: The instrumental view
options.C: The shareholder primacy view
options.D: The legal compliance view

questions.explanation: The instrumental view of stakeholder theory treats attention to stakeholders as a means to an end: satisfying stakeholders improves long-term profitability. The normative view holds that stakeholders have intrinsic moral claims regardless of financial benefit. Shareholder primacy rejects broader stakeholder duties.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: Under English law, section 172 of the Companies Act 2006 requires directors to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. Which of the following must directors also have regard to in doing so?

options.A: The personal political views of the majority shareholder
options.B: The profits of the company's competitors
options.C: The impact of the company's operations on the community and the environment
options.D: The directors' own personal tax position

questions.explanation: Section 172 lists factors that directors must have regard to, including the long-term consequences of decisions, employees' interests, relationships with suppliers and customers, the impact on the community and the environment, high standards of business conduct and acting fairly between members. This is often called 'enlightened shareholder value' and links company law to CSR.

questions.topic: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability
questions.question_text: A company publishes a glossy sustainability report highlighting a small tree-planting project while its main factory continues to breach pollution limits. Which term best describes this behaviour and which principle does it threaten?

options.A: Philanthropy; it demonstrates the top level of Carroll's pyramid
options.B: Triple bottom line reporting; it shows balanced performance
options.C: Stakeholder mapping; it identifies key players
options.D: Greenwashing; it threatens integrity because the reporting is misleading

questions.explanation: Greenwashing is presenting a misleading impression of environmental responsibility through selective disclosure. Accountants associated with such reporting risk breaching integrity, which forbids being associated with misleading information. It is neither genuine philanthropy nor balanced triple bottom line reporting, since it ignores legal breaches at the base of Carroll's pyramid.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Under English law, a business sues a supplier for failing to deliver goods as agreed in their contract. Which statement correctly describes this case?

options.A: It is a civil case in which the claimant seeks a remedy, such as damages, for breach of contract
options.B: It is a criminal case brought by the state to punish the supplier
options.C: The supplier can only be held liable if the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt
options.D: It must be prosecuted by the Crown Prosecution Service on the business's behalf

questions.explanation: Breach of contract is a matter of civil law: the injured party (the claimant) brings the action against the defendant to obtain a remedy such as damages, not to have the defendant punished. Criminal cases are brought by the state, usually through the Crown Prosecution Service, and require proof beyond reasonable doubt. In a civil case the standard of proof is the balance of probabilities.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: In a civil case under English law, what is the standard of proof?

options.A: Beyond reasonable doubt
options.B: Beyond all possible doubt
options.C: On the balance of probabilities
options.D: On the evidence of at least two witnesses

questions.explanation: In civil cases the claimant must prove the case on the balance of probabilities, meaning it is more likely than not. In criminal cases the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, a higher standard because a person's liberty may be at stake.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Under English law, which part of a judgment creates a binding precedent for lower courts?

options.A: The obiter dicta
options.B: The dissenting judgment
options.C: The headnote written by the law reporter
options.D: The ratio decidendi

questions.explanation: The ratio decidendi is the legal reasoning necessary for the decision and is binding on lower courts in later cases with similar material facts. Obiter dicta are things said by the way and are only persuasive. Dissenting judgments and headnotes are not binding.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of delegated (secondary) legislation in the UK?

options.A: An Act of Parliament
options.B: A statutory instrument made by a government minister under powers granted by an Act of Parliament
options.C: A decision of the Supreme Court
options.D: A textbook written by a leading academic

questions.explanation: Delegated legislation is law made by a person or body under authority given by Parliament in an enabling (parent) Act. Statutory instruments, byelaws and Orders in Council are the main forms. An Act is primary legislation, court decisions are case law, and textbooks are at most persuasive.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: A judge interprets a statute by looking at what problem the Act was intended to remedy and interpreting it to address that problem. Which rule of statutory interpretation is being applied?

options.A: The mischief rule
options.B: The literal rule
options.C: The golden rule
options.D: The ejusdem generis rule

questions.explanation: The mischief rule, from Heydon's Case, asks what the law was before the Act, what defect (mischief) it was intended to remedy, and interprets the Act to suppress that mischief. The literal rule gives words their plain meaning, the golden rule modifies a literal meaning to avoid absurdity, and ejusdem generis is a linguistic rule for general words following specific ones.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an advantage of judicial precedent as a source of law?

options.A: It allows judges to ignore earlier decisions they disagree with
options.B: It means that law is always developed quickly in response to new issues
options.C: It requires no written records of decisions
options.D: It provides certainty, because similar cases are decided in a similar way

questions.explanation: Binding precedent promotes certainty and consistency, so people can predict how the courts will decide. Its disadvantages include rigidity, since lower courts must follow decisions they may consider wrong, and slow, case-dependent development. Precedent depends heavily on law reporting.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Why was equity developed in English law?

options.A: To replace Acts of Parliament with judge-made rules
options.B: To create criminal offences not covered by statute
options.C: To provide fairness where the strict rules of common law produced unjust results or inadequate remedies
options.D: To apply religious law in commercial disputes

questions.explanation: Equity developed through the Court of Chancery to mitigate the rigidity of the common law, which offered only damages and could produce unfair outcomes. It introduced discretionary remedies such as specific performance, injunctions and rescission. Where common law and equity conflict, equity prevails.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statement about the relationship between common law and equity is correct?

options.A: Where common law and equity conflict, common law prevails because it is the older system
options.B: Where a rule of common law conflicts with a rule of equity, equity prevails
options.C: Equity has been abolished, so equitable remedies are no longer available
options.D: Equitable remedies are available as of right to any claimant who proves a breach of contract

questions.explanation: Since the Judicature Acts 1873-75 the same courts administer both common law and equity, and where the two conflict, equity prevails. Equity has not been abolished: remedies such as specific performance, injunctions and rescission remain available. They are discretionary, unlike common law damages, which are available as of right once a breach of contract is proved.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following statements about the hierarchy of the courts and precedent is correct?

options.A: The High Court binds the Court of Appeal
options.B: Decisions of the Supreme Court bind all lower courts, but the Supreme Court may depart from its own previous decisions where it appears right to do so
options.C: Magistrates' court decisions create binding precedents for the Crown Court
options.D: The Supreme Court is always bound by its own previous decisions

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court (formerly the House of Lords) is at the top of the domestic hierarchy and binds all lower courts. Since the 1966 Practice Statement it may depart from its previous decisions when it appears right to do so. Lower courts do not bind higher ones, and magistrates' courts do not create binding precedent.

questions.topic: General principles of law: legal systems and sources of law
questions.question_text: Under English law, a seller fails to transfer a piece of land as agreed in a contract. The buyer waits two years, without good reason, before asking the court to order specific performance. What is the most likely outcome?

options.A: The court must order specific performance, because the seller is clearly in breach
options.B: The buyer has lost every remedy, because the limitation period for contract claims is two years
options.C: The court will order specific performance only if the buyer also proves that the seller acted fraudulently
options.D: The court may refuse specific performance, because equitable remedies are discretionary and delay defeats equity, but the buyer can still claim damages at common law

questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy, so it is discretionary and governed by the maxims of equity, including 'delay defeats equity': a claimant who delays unreasonably may be refused it, even for a contract for land where it would otherwise normally be granted. Damages for breach of contract are a common law remedy available as of right. The limitation period for a simple contract is six years under the Limitation Act 1980, not two, and fraud is not a requirement for specific performance.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, a shop displays goods on its shelves with price labels. What is the legal status of the display?

options.A: An offer
options.B: An acceptance
options.C: An invitation to treat
options.D: A binding contract

questions.explanation: Displays of goods in shops are invitations to treat, inviting customers to make offers (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots; Fisher v Bell). The customer makes the offer at the till, and the shop accepts or rejects it. This lets the shop refuse to sell, for example if a price is mislabelled.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following terminates an offer?

options.A: A counter-offer by the offeree
options.B: A request for further information about the terms
options.C: The offeror's private change of mind, not communicated
options.D: The offeree's silence

questions.explanation: A counter-offer rejects the original offer and replaces it with a new one (Hyde v Wrench). A mere request for information does not destroy the offer (Stevenson v McLean). Revocation is only effective when communicated, and silence cannot amount to acceptance or rejection.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is presumed NOT to be intended to create legal relations?

options.A: An agreement between two companies for the supply of goods
options.B: A contract of employment
options.C: An agreement between spouses living together about household expenses
options.D: An agreement to buy a car from a dealer

questions.explanation: In domestic and social agreements there is a rebuttable presumption that the parties do not intend legal relations (Balfour v Balfour). In commercial agreements there is a strong presumption that they do. The presumption can be rebutted by evidence, for example where separated spouses make a formal agreement.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: On 1 March, Ann posts a letter accepting Ben's offer. On 2 March, Ben posts a letter revoking the offer. Ann's letter arrives on 3 March and Ben's arrives on 4 March. Under English law, assuming the postal rule applies, is there a contract?

options.A: No, because Ben revoked the offer before Ann's acceptance arrived
options.B: Yes, but only from 3 March when Ben received the acceptance
options.C: No, because postal acceptances are never valid
options.D: Yes, a contract was formed on 1 March when Ann posted her acceptance

questions.explanation: Under the postal rule, acceptance is complete when a properly addressed and stamped letter is posted (Adams v Lindsell), so a contract arose on 1 March. Revocation is only effective when actually received by the offeree (Byrne v Van Tienhoven), and Ben's revocation arrived after the contract was formed, so it was too late.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statement about consideration is correct?

options.A: Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate
options.B: Consideration must be equal in value to what is received
options.C: Past consideration is always good consideration
options.D: Consideration must move to the promisee from a third party

questions.explanation: The courts will not assess whether a bargain is a good one; consideration need only have some value in the eyes of the law (Chappell v Nestle, where chocolate wrappers were sufficient).
