Past consideration is generally not good consideration (Re McArdle), and consideration must move from the promisee.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: A company advertises: 'We will pay a reward to anyone who returns our lost laptop.' Under English law, what type of offer is this, and how is it accepted?

options.A: An invitation to treat, accepted by contacting the company
options.B: A unilateral offer, accepted by performing the requested act
options.C: A bilateral offer, accepted by written notice before performance
options.D: A counter-offer, accepted by the company paying the reward

questions.explanation: A reward advertisement is a unilateral offer made to the world, which is accepted by performing the stated act, without the need to communicate acceptance in advance (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co). It is not an invitation to treat because the terms are definite and the promisor intends to be bound.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Dee painted Ed's house. A week after the job was finished, Ed promised to pay Dee an extra £300 as a thank you. Under English law, can Dee enforce Ed's promise?

options.A: Yes, because painting a house is valuable consideration
options.B: Yes, because any promise made in writing is enforceable
options.C: No, because Dee's consideration is past
options.D: No, because Dee lacks capacity to contract

questions.explanation: Past consideration, meaning an act completed before the promise was made, is not good consideration (Re McArdle). The exception in Lampleigh v Braithwait requires the act to be done at the promisor's request with an understanding that payment would be made, which is not shown here as the promise is a gratuitous thank you.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statement about the capacity of a minor (a person under 18) to contract is correct?

options.A: A minor is bound to pay a reasonable price for necessaries actually supplied
options.B: A minor can never be bound by any contract
options.C: A minor is bound by all contracts in the same way as an adult
options.D: A minor's contracts are binding only if the minor is over 16

questions.explanation: Contracts for necessaries, meaning goods and services suitable to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements, are binding, and the minor must pay a reasonable price. Beneficial contracts of service are also binding. Many other contracts are not enforceable against the minor.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: A builder agrees to complete work for a fixed price. Midway, the client, worried about delay penalties under its own contract, promises extra payment if the builder finishes on time. The builder does so. Under English law, which case most supports the builder enforcing the extra payment?

options.A: Stilk v Myrick, because performing an existing contractual duty is always good consideration
options.B: Williams v Roffey Bros, because the client obtained a practical benefit and there was no duress
options.C: Foakes v Beer, because part payment of a debt discharges the whole debt
options.D: Balfour v Balfour, because the agreement is commercial

questions.explanation: Performing an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is generally not good consideration (Stilk v Myrick). However, Williams v Roffey Bros held that where the promisor obtains a practical benefit, such as avoiding a penalty clause, and there is no economic duress or fraud, the promise of extra payment can be enforced. Foakes v Beer concerns part payment of debts.

questions.topic: Law of contract: formation
questions.question_text: Under English law, a landlord agreed during a crisis to accept half rent from a tenant. When the crisis ended, the landlord claimed full rent for the future. Which doctrine applied, and with what effect?

options.A: Postal rule; the original rent was reinstated from the date of posting
options.B: Privity of contract; the tenant could not rely on the promise
options.C: Past consideration; the landlord's promise was void from the beginning
options.D: Promissory estoppel; the landlord could not recover the full rent for the crisis period but could revert to full rent on reasonable notice once the crisis ended

questions.explanation: In Central London Property Trust v High Trees House, promissory estoppel prevented the landlord from going back on a promise, relied on by the tenant, to accept reduced rent during the war. The doctrine is suspensory: once the conditions ended, full rent could be claimed for the future. It acts as a shield, not a sword.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, what is the remedy for breach of a warranty?

options.A: Termination of the contract and damages
options.B: Damages only
options.C: Specific performance only
options.D: Rescission of the contract only

questions.explanation: A warranty is a minor term, collateral to the main purpose of the contract, and breach entitles the innocent party to damages only. Breach of a condition, which goes to the root of the contract, allows the innocent party to terminate and claim damages.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, what is the standard limitation period for bringing an action for breach of a simple contract?

options.A: Twelve years from the date the contract was made
options.B: Three years from the date of breach
options.C: One year from the date of breach
options.D: Six years from the date of breach

questions.explanation: Under the Limitation Act 1980, an action for breach of a simple contract must be brought within six years from the date the cause of action accrued, normally the date of breach. For contracts made by deed, the period is twelve years.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is an equitable remedy?

options.A: Specific performance
options.B: Liquidated damages
options.C: Nominal damages
options.D: An action for the price

questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy ordering a party to perform its contractual obligations. Equitable remedies are discretionary and are generally granted only where damages would be inadequate, for example in contracts for land or unique goods. Damages and actions for the price are common law remedies.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: A contract states that the seller will deliver goods by 1 June. On 1 May, the seller tells the buyer it will not deliver at all. Under English law, what is the buyer's position?

options.A: The buyer must wait until 1 June before taking any action
options.B: There is no breach until the goods are due, so the buyer has no remedy
options.C: This is anticipatory breach; the buyer may sue immediately or wait until the performance date
options.D: The contract is automatically discharged by frustration

questions.explanation: When one party indicates before performance is due that it will not perform, this is anticipatory breach. The innocent party may treat the contract as ended and sue immediately (Hochster v De la Tour), or affirm it and wait for the performance date, accepting the risk of later events. Refusal to perform is not frustration.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statement about exclusion clauses is correct?

options.A: Any exclusion clause is valid if it appears anywhere in a signed contract, regardless of statute
options.B: An exclusion clause printed on a receipt given after the contract is made is always incorporated
options.C: Ambiguities in an exclusion clause are interpreted in favour of the party relying on it
options.D: Liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence cannot be excluded

questions.explanation: Under statute (the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 for business contracts, and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 for consumer contracts), liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded. Notice must be given before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court Hotel), and ambiguities are construed against the party relying on the clause (contra proferentem).

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, the rule in Hadley v Baxendale concerns which aspect of damages?

options.A: Mitigation: the claimant must take reasonable steps to reduce the loss
options.B: Penalties: a clause imposing a disproportionate sum is unenforceable
options.C: Remoteness: losses are recoverable if they arise naturally from the breach or were in the reasonable contemplation of both parties when contracting
options.D: Nominal damages: a small sum is awarded where no loss is proven

questions.explanation: Hadley v Baxendale established the two limbs of remoteness: losses arising naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, and losses that may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting as the probable result of breach. Other losses are too remote to recover.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Kiran agreed to buy machinery from Lee for £40,000. Lee breached the contract by failing to deliver. Kiran bought an identical machine elsewhere for £46,000. Kiran also lost profits of £3,000 that were in both parties' reasonable contemplation. Under English law, what damages can Kiran most likely claim?
questions.explanation: Expectation damages aim to put Kiran in the position she would have been in had the contract been performed. Extra cost of a substitute machine = £46,000 - £40,000 = £6,000. Add the foreseeable lost profit of £3,000, giving £6,000 + £3,000 = £9,000. She cannot recover the full £46,000, because she would have paid £40,000 in any event.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, what is the effect of a valid liquidated damages clause?

options.A: The innocent party recovers the agreed sum on breach, regardless of whether actual loss is higher or lower
options.B: The innocent party must prove its actual loss before recovering anything
options.C: The clause is void because damages can only be set by a court
options.D: The innocent party recovers the agreed sum plus any additional actual loss

questions.explanation: A liquidated damages clause fixes in advance the sum payable on breach. If valid, the agreed sum is recoverable whether actual loss turns out to be greater or smaller, and the innocent party need not prove its loss. Following Cavendish Square Holding v Makdessi (2015), a clause is an unenforceable penalty only if it imposes a detriment out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance; it no longer has to be a strict genuine pre-estimate of loss.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: A singer contracts to perform at a concert but refuses to attend. The organiser asks the court to order her to perform. Under English law, what is the court most likely to do?

options.A: Order specific performance, because it is available as of right for any breach
options.B: Refuse specific performance, because the courts will not order performance of contracts for personal services, and award damages instead
options.C: Order the singer to be imprisoned until she performs
options.D: Refuse any remedy, because the organiser should have included a penalty clause

questions.explanation: Specific performance is discretionary and is not granted for contracts of personal service, because forcing someone to work would be oppressive and impossible to supervise. The organiser would be awarded damages. In some cases an injunction may restrain the singer from performing elsewhere in breach of an express negative stipulation.

questions.topic: Law of contract: terms, breach and remedies
questions.question_text: Under English law, a ship is chartered for 24 months. Due to the owner's breach of a term requiring the ship to be 'seaworthy', the ship is out of service for five weeks. The term could be broken in trivial or serious ways. How is the term classified and what is the charterer's remedy?

options.A: A condition; the charterer may always terminate the contract
options.B: A warranty; the charterer may never terminate, whatever the consequences
options.C: An exclusion clause; the charterer has no remedy
options.D: An innominate term; the charterer can claim damages but can only terminate if the breach deprives it of substantially the whole benefit of the contract

questions.explanation: Following Hong Kong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, a term that can be broken in ways ranging from trivial to serious is innominate. The remedy depends on the seriousness of the consequences: termination is available only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit intended, otherwise damages only. Losing five weeks of a 24-month charter is unlikely to meet that test, so the charterer would be limited to damages.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is an implied duty owed by an employee to an employer?

options.A: To obey reasonable and lawful orders
options.B: To provide the employer with a safe system of work
options.C: To pay the employer's taxes
options.D: To provide a reference for other employees

questions.explanation: Implied duties of employees include obeying reasonable and lawful orders, exercising reasonable care and skill, and acting in good faith (fidelity). Providing a safe system of work is a duty owed by the employer. Tax and references are not implied employee duties.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is an implied common law duty of an employer?

options.A: To provide employees with a pension in every case
options.B: To give every employee an annual pay rise
options.C: To take reasonable care for the health and safety of employees
options.D: To guarantee employment for life

questions.explanation: Employers have implied duties to pay agreed wages, take reasonable care for employees' safety (competent staff, safe equipment, safe premises and safe system of work), and maintain mutual trust and confidence. Pensions, pay rises and lifetime employment are not implied by common law.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: What is the main legal basis of a claim for wrongful dismissal under English law?

options.A: Breach of statutory rights under unfair dismissal legislation
options.B: The tort of negligence
options.C: Criminal law
options.D: Breach of the contract of employment, typically dismissal without proper notice

questions.explanation: Wrongful dismissal is a common law claim for breach of contract, usually where the employer dismisses without giving the notice required by the contract or statute. Unfair dismissal is a separate statutory claim focusing on the reason for and fairness of the dismissal.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which test is used to decide whether a person is an employee or an independent contractor, looking at all aspects of the relationship together?

options.A: The postal rule
options.B: The multiple (economic reality) test
options.C: The but-for test
options.D: The reasonable person test

questions.explanation: Courts use the multiple or economic reality test (Ready Mixed Concrete v Minister of Pensions), considering control, mutuality of obligation, whether the person provides their own equipment, bears financial risk, can delegate work, and how they are paid and taxed. No single factor is decisive. The control and integration tests are earlier, narrower tests.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is NOT a potentially fair reason for dismissal under the Employment Rights Act 1996?

options.A: The employee's membership of a trade union
options.B: The employee's conduct
options.C: Redundancy
options.D: The employee's capability or qualifications

questions.explanation: Under section 98 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, the potentially fair reasons are capability or qualifications, conduct, redundancy, contravention of a statutory duty or restriction, and some other substantial reason. Dismissal because of trade union membership or activities is automatically unfair (Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, s152). Even with a fair reason, the employer must act reasonably and follow a fair procedure.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, an employee resigns because the employer, without consent, cuts her pay by 30%. Which claim is she most likely to bring?

options.A: Redundancy
options.B: Frustration of contract
options.C: Constructive dismissal
options.D: Breach of the duty of fidelity

questions.explanation: Constructive dismissal occurs where the employer commits a repudiatory breach of a fundamental term and the employee resigns in response (Western Excavating v Sharp). A significant unilateral pay cut is such a breach. The resignation is treated as a dismissal, which may then be unfair.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is the correct definition of redundancy?

options.A: Dismissal wholly or mainly because the employer ceases business, or the need for employees to do work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished
options.B: Dismissal because of the employee's poor performance
options.C: Dismissal because of the employee's misconduct
options.D: Any dismissal where the employee is paid in lieu of notice

questions.explanation: Under section 139 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, redundancy arises where the employer has ceased, or intends to cease, carrying on the business or the business in the place where the employee was employed, or where the need for employees to carry out work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished. Performance and conduct are separate reasons for dismissal.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, an employee has been continuously employed by the same employer for 7 complete years. What is the minimum statutory notice the employer must give to terminate the contract, assuming the contract does not provide for longer?

options.A: 1 week
options.B: 7 weeks
options.C: 12 weeks
options.D: 1 month

questions.explanation: Under section 86 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, an employer must give an employee with between one month and two years' continuous service at least one week's notice, and after two years one week for each complete year of service, up to a maximum of 12 weeks. For 7 complete years: 7 x 1 week = 7 weeks, which is below the 12-week cap. A longer contractual notice period would prevail.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following remedies for unfair dismissal involves the employer re-employing the employee in a different but comparable job?

options.A: Reinstatement
options.B: Basic award
options.C: Re-engagement
options.D: Specific performance

questions.explanation: Reinstatement means returning the employee to the same job as if never dismissed. Re-engagement means re-employment with the employer, an associated employer or a successor in comparable or suitable employment. Compensation consists of a basic award and a compensatory award. Specific performance is not ordered for employment contracts.

questions.topic: Law of employment
questions.question_text: Under English law, an employer, without good reason, humiliates an employee publicly and repeatedly undermines her authority. Which implied term is most likely to be breached?

options.A: The duty of fidelity
options.B: The duty to obey lawful orders
options.C: The duty to exercise reasonable care and skill in performing work
options.D: The duty to maintain mutual trust and confidence

questions.explanation: Employers must not, without reasonable and proper cause, conduct themselves in a manner likely to destroy or seriously damage the relationship of trust and confidence (Malik v BCCI). Serious breach can justify resignation and a constructive dismissal claim. Fidelity, obedience and care and skill are duties owed by employees.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, what is the principle established in Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd?

options.A: Members are personally liable for all of a company's debts
options.B: Directors must hold shares in the company
options.C: A registered company is a separate legal person, distinct from its members
options.D: A company cannot be owned by a single person

questions.explanation: Salomon established that a properly incorporated company has a separate legal personality from its members, even where one person holds almost all the shares. Consequently, the company owns its property and is liable for its own debts, and members' liability is limited to any amount unpaid on their shares.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, which type of resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of the votes cast?

options.A: A special resolution
options.B: An ordinary resolution
options.C: A board resolution
options.D: A written resolution of a public company

questions.explanation: Under section 283 of the Companies Act 2006, a special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% (of the votes cast at a meeting, or of the total voting rights of eligible members for a private company's written resolution), while an ordinary resolution under section 282 needs a simple majority (more than 50%). Board resolutions are decisions of directors, and public companies cannot use the statutory written resolution procedure.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, which of the following is a key difference between a public company (plc) and a private company?

options.A: Only a private company has limited liability
options.B: Only a public company has a separate legal personality
options.C: Only a private company must file accounts
options.D: Only a public company may offer its shares to the public

questions.explanation: A private company is prohibited from offering its shares to the public; a public company may do so and may seek a listing. Both can have limited liability and separate legal personality, and both must file accounts with the Registrar of Companies.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, a promoter signs a contract on behalf of a company before the company is incorporated. Who is liable on the contract?

options.A: The company, automatically, once it is incorporated
options.B: The promoter personally, subject to any agreement to the contrary
options.C: No one, because the contract is void
options.D: The Registrar of Companies

questions.explanation: Under section 51 of the Companies Act 2006, a pre-incorporation contract takes effect as one made with the person purporting to act for the company, who is personally liable, subject to any agreement to the contrary (see also Kelner v Baxter). A company cannot ratify a contract made before it existed; it would need to enter a new contract (novation).

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, how can the members of a company remove a director before the end of his term of office?

options.A: By ordinary resolution at a general meeting, with special notice given to the company
options.B: By special resolution passed as a written resolution
options.C: Only by a court order
options.D: Only if the articles expressly permit removal

questions.explanation: Section 168 of the Companies Act 2006 allows members to remove a director by ordinary resolution at a meeting, notwithstanding anything in the articles or any agreement with the director. Special notice (at least 28 days' notice to the company under section 312) must be given, and the director has the right to be heard and to make written representations (section 169). A written resolution cannot be used for this purpose (section 288).

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statutory duty of directors is breached when a director diverts a business opportunity that came to him as a director to his own private company?

options.A: The duty to act within powers
options.B: The duty to exercise independent judgement
options.C: The duty to keep accounting records
options.D: The duty to avoid conflicts of interest

questions.explanation: Section 175 of the Companies Act 2006 requires a director to avoid situations in which he has, or could have, a direct or indirect interest that conflicts with the company's interests, including exploiting property, information or opportunity. This applies even if the company could not itself take the opportunity, unless the conflict is properly authorised.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, a company issues 10,000 £1 ordinary shares at a price of £3.50 each, fully paid in cash. What amount is credited to the share premium account?
questions.explanation: Share capital is credited with the nominal value: 10,000 x £1 = £10,000. The excess of issue price over nominal value goes to share premium: 10,000 x (£3.50 - £1.00) = 10,000 x £2.50 = £25,000. Total cash received is £35,000 (£10,000 + £25,000). The share premium account is subject to capital maintenance rules.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, which statement about a floating charge is correct?

options.A: It attaches to a specific identified asset, which the company cannot sell without the lender's consent
options.B: It is a charge over a class of assets that changes over time, such as inventory, which the company can deal with in the ordinary course of business until crystallisation
options.C: It can only be created by a sole trader
options.D: It ranks ahead of all fixed charges on insolvency

questions.explanation: A floating charge hovers over a changing class of assets and allows the company to deal with them freely until an event, such as liquidation or default, causes it to crystallise into a fixed charge. A fixed charge attaches to specific assets. Fixed charges rank ahead of floating charges, and only companies and LLPs can create floating charges.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, the members of a private company want to change its articles of association. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The articles can be altered by special resolution, and the alteration must be made bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole
options.B: The articles can only be altered with the consent of every member
options.C: The articles can be altered by a resolution of the directors alone
options.D: The articles can never be altered once the company is registered

questions.explanation: Section 21 of the Companies Act 2006 allows a company to amend its articles by special resolution, subject to any entrenched provisions. The courts have held that the alteration must be made bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole (Allen v Gold Reefs of West Africa). Unanimity is only needed if an entrenchment provision requires it.

questions.topic: Company administration and finance
questions.question_text: Under English law, a private company is solvent. Its accumulated realised profits are £180,000 and its accumulated realised losses are £70,000. It also has an unrealised revaluation gain of £50,000. What is the maximum dividend it may lawfully pay?
questions.explanation: Under section 830 of the Companies Act 2006, distributions may only be made out of profits available for the purpose: accumulated realised profits (not previously distributed or capitalised) less accumulated realised losses (not previously written off). £180,000 - £70,000 = £110,000. The unrealised revaluation gain of £50,000 cannot be distributed. (A public company must also satisfy the net assets test in section 831.)
